text: The Family Portrait (also known as the Brunswick Family Portrait) is a painting by the Dutch painter Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669).
The work is in the collection of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum in Braunschweig.
The work shows an unknown married couple with three children.
The youngest child sits on its mother's lap.
The two other children, one of them a daughter holding a basket of flowers, are evidently turned towards each other in conversation.
The figure of the father, in the background of the group, holds a red flower in his hand.
The palette consists mainly of brown, green and intense shades of red.
The paint is mostly applied thickly (impasto) with coarse brushwork, but also with the palette knife, especially in the depiction of the mother and her youngest child.
In this section the picture looks almost like a relief.
No details of the surrounding room can be made out.
The picture is limited entirely to the depiction of the people.
The artist does without any representative elements such as splendid furniture or proud, self-confident poses.
The atmosphere conveys the impression of a happy situation.
The painting, in oil on canvas, was probably executed between 1665 and 1668.
The family portrait is therefore one of Rembrandt's last works.
The flower basket bears the artist's signature (Rembrandt f).
He did not, however, date the time of completion.
The work was acquired by Duke Anton Ulrich of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel (1633–1714), the founder of today's museum, which is named after him.
The duke bought his paintings mainly in Amsterdam, the leading art market of the time.
The painting is documented in the picture gallery of the ducal residence at Salzdahlum Palace from 1737.
The people depicted have not been identified.
It is also unknown whether the painting was a commission or a free work.
It is sometimes interpreted as the design of a counter-idyll to Rembrandt's own family situation.
Rembrandt's son Titus died in 1668; his companion Hendrickje Stoffels († 1663), his wife Saskia († 1642) and other children had died before.
As late as the mid-19th century the picture bore the title Rembrandt with His Family.
If, however, it was a commission, it is assumed that it was not accepted by those who commissioned it.
Until the early 20th century the so-called Brunswick Family Portrait was considered "strange" and was even interpreted as evidence of Rembrandt's declining artistic ability.
The painter Lovis Corinth, by contrast, admired the work as a "Brunswick jewel".

Today the work is considered a masterly late work which, for some art historians, together with paintings such as The Jewish Bride and the late self-portraits, documents Rembrandt's reputation as "the first modern painter".
The Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum ranks the Family Portrait by Rembrandt van Rijn (inventory number GG 238) as the most important of its five works by the Dutch master.
The Girl with the Wine Glass is an oil painting by Jan Vermeer, painted in 1658–1659.
The genre picture, 78 centimetres high and 67.5 centimetres wide, shows a young girl with a wine glass in her hand and two men in a room.
Anton Ulrich, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, acquired the painting around 1696.
Today it hangs in the Old Masters collection of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum in Braunschweig, which is named after him.
The picture shows a scene in a room.
In the foreground sits a girl with a wine glass in her hand; a young man bends down towards her and holds her hand, as if urging her to drink the glass soon.
Another man sits at the back left, in the corner of the room, behind a table on which there are a wine jug, a silver plate with some fruit and a white cloth.
He seems to have fallen asleep.
The young woman's dress is a luminous red that stands out from the other colours in the room.
The clothing of the two men, on the other hand, is rather pale and so fits much better into the colour range of the room.
In the background of the painting a portrait of a man hangs on the wall; it looks dark because of the shadow on the wall.
On the left side of the picture there is a slightly open window.
It is a leaded glass window with a coloured coat of arms in the middle.
The man seems to want to seduce the woman.
Whether he does so for himself or on behalf of the man in the background is left open.
She looks sideways in embarrassment, towards the viewer.
The second man in the background, however, is probably no longer quite able to follow the scene.
He seems to have already grown tired from enjoying the drink.
It is not clear whether the drink is wine or an aphrodisiac, which the citrus fruits might suggest.
The man in the painting in the background could be the absent husband, looking at his wife in admonition.
But the man in the corner could also be the drunken husband, dazed and blind to what is happening in the room.
His portrait, however, still keeps watch.
In the stained glass window the allegory of Temperantia, Temperance, one of the cardinal virtues, can be recognised.
From 10 September 2021 to 2 January 2022 the picture was shown in Dresden as one of ten paintings by Vermeer in the exhibition Johannes Vermeer.
On Reflection.

In a video series with contributions from all the lenders, Silke Gatenbröcker, head of the picture gallery of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, spoke about the relationship between manner of painting and meaning in this picture.
In 2017 The Girl with the Wine Glass appeared on a German 70-cent special postage stamp issued in the series "Treasures from German Museums".
Judith with the Head of Holofernes is a painting by Peter Paul Rubens, made in Antwerp around 1616 to 1618.
It shows a scene from the Book of Judith, which has been depicted by several artists in painting or sculpture.
Stylistically it belongs to the Flemish Baroque.
Rubens depicts the biblical heroine Judith in the upper centre of the picture as a sensual young woman, her breast almost entirely bared, who looks at the viewer.
Her body also radiates strength and vitality.
In her right hand she holds a sword with which she has just cut off the head of Holofernes, the commander of the enemy army.
With her left hand she holds the head, which is shown in the lower centre of the picture, its face also turned towards the viewer, by a tuft of hair.
On the right side of the picture stands an old maidservant, who reaches for the severed head with her left hand and holds in her right hand a burning candle that lights the scene.
The maidservant is dressed in a garment with red sleeves and looks at the head of Holofernes.
In the background, parts of the commander's armour can be seen.
The painting, measuring 120 × 111 cm, has been documented in the gallery of Salzdahlum Palace since around 1700.
It is owned by the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum under inventory number GG 87 and is part of the cultural heritage of Lower Saxony.
Rubens probably made the painting for study purposes.
It was certainly not a commission, since he did not use high-quality wood as a support but a simple wooden panel.
While working on it he changed the composition several times and enlarged the picture surface by attaching further pieces of wood.
He kept the picture in his studio for a long time.
The Assyrian king Nebuchadnezzar ordered his commander-in-chief Holofernes to subdue several cities in Asia Minor and Syria.
When the inhabitants of the town of Bethulia steadfastly defended themselves, he had the water supply cut off to force the inhabitants to surrender.
Judith, a Jewish widow from the besieged town, was considered rich and graceful.
Trusting in God, she decided to save her home town and her people.
By a ruse she gained access to the enemy camp and the favour of Holofernes.
Accompanied by her maid, she brought some jugs of wine to the commander's tent.
He was very taken with her beauty and thought Judith was a deserter, so he quartered her in his camp.
Shortly afterwards he called her to him to spend a night of love together.
At the banquet held beforehand, Judith had Holofernes poured a great deal of wine.
When he had fallen asleep, Judith killed him with his own sword, so as to save her people from destruction.
After the deed the women put the head of Holofernes in a sack and carried it out of the camp.
On their return to their home town they were received with rejoicing, and the enemy troops fled at the sight of the beheaded Holofernes.

As early as around 1610 Rubens painted, in a picture with full-length figures, the preceding scene, in which Judith had half severed Holofernes' neck with a first stroke of the sword and his body rears up one last time.
A similar picture with this scene is in the National Museum in Warsaw.
He also recorded in paintings the following scene, in which the head of Holofernes is stowed in a sack so as to carry it out of the camp unseen.
The Death of Cleopatra is an oil painting on panel (94.7 x 73 cm) by Rosso Fiorentino, datable to around 1525 and kept in the Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museum in Braunschweig.
The work is attributed to Rosso Fiorentino's stay in Rome, when he came into contact with ancient statuary.

Giorgio Vasari, in the preface to the third part of the Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, reports how the ancient models offered by the sculptures discovered in those years (such as the Laocoön Group, the Farnese Hercules and all the others) had provided the impetus for the leap in quality of the Renaissance in the first decades of the sixteenth century, listing among others also the "Cleopatra", that is, the Sleeping Ariadne now in the Vatican Museums, mistaken for the queen of Egypt because of a bracelet in the shape of snakes, which were thought to be the fatal asp.

Rosso drew inspiration precisely from this famous statue, formerly in the collection of Angelo Maffei, then acquired by Julius II in 1512 and placed in the Belvedere courtyard, for his Cleopatra, taking up its pose with the head tilted slightly backwards and resting on the wrist, with the elbow bent like a compass.

One of Rosso's most copied panels, and the first known secular subject in his catalogue before he arrived at Fontainebleau, it shows some features typical of his painting, such as the shot-coloured draperies, the languor, and the facial features "in the Greek manner", like those of the queen, who appears closely related to the Virgin in the Deposition of Sansepolcro.

Despite this, the panel has gone through a long process of attribution, which even led to its being considered a seventeenth-century work, perhaps from the circle of Cagnacci, because of its pervasive luminism.
Unusual is the figure of the young girl who rushes in from the left with her hands joined and raised to her neck, her face partly in shadow.

The delicately blended tones, above all of Cleopatra's voluptuous body, are here and there interrupted by dry, quick touches, such as the swollen nipples or the mask that can be glimpsed in the half-light under the damask cushions on the right.
Aurora (in German: Morgenlandschaft) is a painting by the German painter Adam Elsheimer.
It measures 17 cm high and 22.5 cm wide, and is painted in oil on copper.
It dates from around 1606 and is in the Herzog Anton Ulrich-Museum (Kunstmuseum des Landes Niedersachsen) in Brunswick (inv. no. 549).
Adam Elsheimer (Frankfurt, 1578 – Rome, 1610) was a German painter who settled in Italy in 1598, at the age of twenty.

He devoted himself mainly to landscape painting and, despite his small output due to his early death, his work was the forerunner of a way of understanding landscape that would strongly influence Baroque landscape painting.
He made numerous landscapes, generally of small size and painted in oil on copper.
They often have a religious or mythological subject, although the figures are small in relation to the landscape, which is the true protagonist of his works.
His style shows a certain influence of Caravaggio's tenebrism, as well as of Flemish painting.
His work influenced Rubens, Claude Lorrain and Rembrandt.
Elsheimer initiated a late-Mannerist style of landscape, exploiting the poetic resources offered by light illuminating an entire landscape, as well as the sensational effects of dawn and dusk.
The Frankfurt artist stood out for his studies of light in landscape, with an interest in the light of sunrise and sunset, as well as night lighting and atmospheric effects such as fog and mist.
His light was strange and intense, with an enamel-like appearance typical of German painting, in a tradition that runs from Lukas Moser to Albrecht Altdorfer.

The first owner of this painting was Hendrik Goudt, Elsheimer's pupil and patron, who published it as an engraving in Utrecht in 1613, the date at which it appears for the first time with the title Aurora.
This work presents a wooded landscape at dawn, in which a dark mass of vegetation appears on the left side, descending towards the right.
In the lower left corner appears a solitary figure, probably a shepherd.
On the right side the landscape opens towards the horizon, and a building can be glimpsed in the lower right corner.

The upper part of the painting is taken up by a sky streaked with a few clouds, in which the first light of dawn appears; its greatest brightness is in the central part of the painting, above the mountainous horizon, and it fades upwards into a darker blue.
The building in the lower right corner has traditionally been identified with the Villa of Maecenas.
Some historians have suggested that the scene might represent the myth of Acis and Galatea, but there is no reference to confirm it.

The depiction of dawn was not yet very common in Elsheimer's time: until the seventeenth century dawn appeared only in small pieces of landscape, generally behind a door or a window, and it was never used to light the foreground.
The light of dawn generally has soft, blurred effects, so it was little used until the appearance of Leonardo's aerial perspective.
However, after Elsheimer and other artists such as Claude Lorrain or Salvator Rosa, dawn became a subject of interest for painters.

In his Dictionary of the Fine Arts of Design (1797), Francesco Milizia states that "dawn gently colours the edges of bodies, begins to dispel the darkness of the night, and the air, still heavy with vapours, leaves objects wavering...
But the sun has not yet appeared, so the shadows cannot be very marked.

All bodies must share in the freshness of the air and remain in a kind of half-tone. [...] The background of the sky should be a dark blue... so that the vault of the sky stands out better and the source of light appears: there the sky will be coloured a vermilion red from a certain height, with alternating gold and silver bands, which will lose their liveliness as they move away from the place where the light rises." For Milizia, the light of dawn was the most suitable for painting landscapes.
The story of Judith and Holofernes has been recorded in the Book of Judith from the Old Testament.
The book tells of the fate of the young, wealthy and beautiful widow Judith.
Her small nation was besieged by the Assyrian prince Holofernes.
In order to save her people Judith resorted to a ploy.
She gained access to the enemy's army camp, bewitched Holofernes with her seductive female charms and obtained his confidence.
When she was invited to a banquet there she waited until they had been left alone and the drunken Holofernes had gone to sleep.
Then she took his sword and beheaded him.
What was considered in the Middle Ages as an example of a woman's wiles, the magical power of seduction, was classified in the Baroque as a courageous sacrifice.
Judith had jeopardised her own life to rescue her people.
The story of Judith and Holofernes was a popular subject in the visual arts and Peter Paul Rubens as the leading Flemish master of the Baroque created something completely new with this picture.
Rubens portrays the moment right after the deed in extremely dramatic light.
However Judith's triumph is not undisturbed.
Her face with the red cheeks brightly lit up from below indicates a high level of tension.
Judith looks at us directly and seems to ask how such a deed can be judged.
A person had to die but can the end justify the means?
Much is obscure about this picture.
We do not know who these people are who shine warmly out of the twilight.
We do know, however, that Rembrandt is not depicting here his own eventful family life.
In this painting parents and children treat each other in a natural and lively way and typify an affectionate attachment to one another.
Perhaps this is in fact not the portrait of a real family but represents an ideal picture.
The woman, who embodies the mother here, also appears in other paintings by Rembrandt, both as a mother as well as a wife.
In our family she forms together with the smallest child on her lap a close unit.
The child plays happily with its rattle in its hand.
The family is apparently in a garden as a bushy, deciduous hedge is shown behind them.
The fact that it is a garden is also indicated by the motif of the flowers which the eldest girl is carrying in a basket.
The smaller sister smiles at her happily while the father places a red carnation into the basket, a sign of love between man and woman.
This late work originated about a year before Rembrandt's death.
The artist had lost many family members in the course of his lifetime.
The intimate get-together of a family in one of his last great paintings is timeless and touches us today in a very special way.
Sunk into the cushions, her head supported by her arm, this is how Cleopatra slumbers towards her death.
The bite of the small snake that is coiled around the top of her arm is the cause of this event.
A servant appears from the left, lamenting the death of her mistress.
Cleopatra reigned as the last Egyptian queen and at the same time as the last female pharaoh.
The ancient pictorial theme of the suicide of Cleopatra, who had herself been bitten by a poison snake, enjoyed great popularity in the Renaissance and the Baroque age.
Not least, it was a welcome reason for depicting seductive female beauty.
Rosso Fiorentino too does not shy from putting the legendary queen center stage almost completely naked.
Only a cloth lies over her lap and covers her abdomen.
Life is draining out of her body.
The head that has fallen back into the nape of her neck as well as the face with open mouth and half-closed eyelids, endow the dying woman with a special sensuous expression.
Light falls in from above left and makes the face and body of the dying woman shine in perfect white.
Cleopatra looks like a figure sculpted from marble.
Indeed, the artist got to know the collection of ancient sculptures in the Belvedere Court of the Vatican in Rome when he spent some time there.
He adopted certain motifs from famous sculptures for his paintings.
"Be careful" is what we would like to call over to the young woman, for a man is encouraging her to drink while looking at her, lurking.
The peeled lemon on the table was often seen by contemporaries as a symbol of injured innocence.
Perhaps, too, it is a scene from the life of the upper bourgeoisie in Holland.
In this context, the hand of the young woman with the wine glass is interesting.
She is holding the glass from underneath in an elegant way.
Is she getting a lesson in cultivated behavior?
The young woman turns to us directly with a smile.
It is, however, not clear whether her smile is an indicator of childlike innocence or part of a game with the advances of the man.
The picture does not give a clear message.
The painting was first called 'Merry Company', then 'Young Man with His Mistress', and 'The Coquette'.
Today's title "The Girl with the Wine Glass" neutralizes the scene and so opens up the possibility of our own interpretation.
Vermeer deals in a masterly way with composition and color.
The incomparably diffused daylight, as only he was able to transpose onto the canvas, has been the basis of his fame to this day.
As he worked very slowly and carefully, he presumably only completed 36 works in his whole life.
These, however, can be counted as being amongst the best works of 17th-century Dutch painting.
On a small copper plate the Frankfurt painter Adam Elsheimer unfolds a breathtaking landscape.
Our eyes roam from the wooded hillside over to a wide, valley facing south with a river and blue mountains on the horizon.
In Roman mythology Aurora is the goddess of dawn and the picture does indeed show a sunrise.
Elsheimer's special achievement is however, to transform the ancient divine allegory into a natural phenomenon.
Elsheimer realizes the transformation between the dark of the night and the light of the day in the smallest possible format.
The monumentality of the landscape beneath the high sky and the depiction of the light are the actual sensation in the picture.
Elsheimer can be considered as one of the most important painters of German origin in the early 17th century.
Only after his death did the paintings become well known through the copper plate engravings of his student Hendrick Goud.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe also knew the copper plate copy of Elsheimer's Morning Landscape and in a well-known German poem to Princess Augusta of Saxon Weimar, he was inspired by this very engraving.
*Every poplar high above,*
*Every shrub in fragrant love,*
*Turns to look where you have gone.*
*Mountains gaze from over there,*
*Glow with joy in clearer air—*
*Yet the lovely day is silent, withdrawn.*
*New delights and songs arise*
*To greet you—come, regrace our skies,*
*As spring returns to light.*
